title: Type 1 diabetes: outpatient management (adult)
subject: endocrinology
summary: Confirm with islet autoantibodies, start basal-bolus analogue insulin at about 0.5 units/kg/day (half basal), offer CGM and automated insulin delivery from diagnosis, aim for HbA1c below 7% with time in range above 70%, prescribe glucagon, and teach never to stop basal insulin on sick days.

sections.title: Diagnose and classify
items: Features favouring type 1 in adults: age under 35, BMI below 25 kg/m2, unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and glucose above 360 mg/dL (20 mmol/L) at presentation. Adult onset is common and is often mislabelled as type 2.
Measure islet autoantibodies at diagnosis: GAD first, then IA-2 and/or ZnT8 if negative. About 5 to 10% of people with type 1 diabetes are antibody-negative.

If the type is uncertain after 3 years, measure random C-peptide (with paired glucose, within 5 hours of eating), and always before stopping insulin: 600 pmol/L or more suggests type 2 or monogenic diabetes; low or absent confirms severe insulin deficiency.

Consider monogenic diabetes with onset under 35, HbA1c below 7.5% (58 mmol/mol) at diagnosis, a parent with diabetes, or antibody-negative disease with preserved C-peptide; test for neonatal diabetes if diagnosed before 6 months of age.
Ketoacidosis at presentation or at any time: manage as diabetic ketoacidosis (see the DKA protocol).

sections.title: Insulin regimen
items: Use physiological replacement from diagnosis: a basal analogue plus rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting analogue with meals (multiple daily injections), or pump therapy. Analogues are preferred over human insulins to reduce hypoglycaemia (ADA).

Typical starting total daily dose (TDD) 0.5 units/kg/day in metabolically stable adults, lower (0.2 to 0.6 units/kg/day) in the new-onset partial remission phase; usual range 0.4 to 1.0 units/kg/day, higher in puberty, pregnancy and illness.
Give about half the TDD as basal insulin (glargine or degludec once daily; detemir may need twice daily) and half as mealtime insulin divided between meals.

Teach carbohydrate counting with an insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio, correction doses using an insulin sensitivity factor, and adjustment for fat, protein, exercise and alcohol. Structured education (such as DAFNE) reduces severe hypoglycaemia.
Where analogues are unaffordable, twice-daily NPH with regular insulin before meals is an acceptable alternative, with a higher risk of hypoglycaemia.
Review and adjust ratios and basal doses from glucose data at least every 3 to 6 months (ADA).

sections.title: Glucose monitoring and technology
items: Offer CGM from diagnosis to all adults on insulin (ADA 2026).

Automated insulin delivery (hybrid closed loop) is the preferred insulin delivery method in type 1 diabetes (ADA 2026, ADA/EASD 2026). Do not require a C-peptide level, antibodies or a minimum insulin duration before starting a pump or AID.
Review a standardised CGM report (ambulatory glucose profile) at every visit.
Pump and AID users need a written backup injection plan: any interruption of insulin delivery causes rapid ketosis.
Without CGM, use fingerstick glucose monitoring before meals and at bedtime, and before driving and exercise.

sections.title: Glycaemic targets
items: HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol) for most adults; below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) if achievable without significant hypoglycaemia; less stringent with frailty, limited life expectancy or impaired hypoglycaemia awareness.

CGM: time in range 70 to 180 mg/dL (3.9 to 10.0 mmol/L) above 70%; time below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) under 4% (under 1% in older adults); below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) under 1%; above 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) under 5%.
Fingerstick goals: pre-meal 80 to 130 mg/dL (4.4 to 7.2 mmol/L) and peak after meals below 180 mg/dL (10.0 mmol/L).
HbA1c every 3 months when not at goal or after treatment changes, otherwise at least twice a year.

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia
items: Level 1: glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) but 54 mg/dL or above. Level 2: below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L). Level 3: altered mental or physical state needing help from another person.

Treat with about 15 g of glucose, recheck after 15 minutes and repeat until above 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L); AID users often need only 5 to 15 g. Follow with a snack or meal containing about 20 g carbohydrate.
Confirm recovery with a fingerstick: CGM lags 5 to 15 minutes and encourages overtreatment.

Prescribe glucagon for everyone on insulin (ready-to-use preparations preferred) and train family members. If unable to swallow: glucagon 1 mg IM or SC, or nasal glucagon 3 mg; IV glucose in hospital.
Screen for impaired awareness at least yearly (Gold score 4 or more, or symptoms only below 54 mg/dL): relax targets, strictly avoid hypoglycaemia, and use CGM with alerts or AID.

sections.title: Sick days, driving and pregnancy
items: Never stop or omit basal insulin, even when not eating. During illness check glucose often and ketones (blood testing preferred), particularly when glucose is above 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L); give extra rapid-acting insulin as per the personal sick-day plan and keep up fluids and carbohydrate.
Seek urgent care for persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids down, glucose or ketones not improving with extra insulin, blood ketones 3.0 mmol/L or more, drowsiness or breathlessness.
SGLT2 inhibitors are not approved for type 1 diabetes in the US and markedly increase DKA risk; avoid outside specialist care.
Driving: check glucose before driving and every 2 hours on long journeys; do not drive with low glucose. Follow local licensing rules.
Plan pregnancy: preconception HbA1c below 6.5% if safe, folic acid, stop ACE inhibitors, ARBs and statins, and retinal screening before and during pregnancy.
Obesity with type 1 diabetes: GLP-1 based therapy or metabolic surgery may be considered with shared decision-making (ADA 2026).

sections.title: Annual review and screening
items: Every visit: weight, blood pressure, injection or infusion sites for lipohypertrophy, hypoglycaemia history and glucose data.

Kidney (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR) and neuropathy screening yearly from 5 years after diagnosis; dilated eye examination within 5 years of diagnosis, then every 1 to 2 years; yearly foot examination.
TSH, coeliac serology and vitamin B12 at least once after diagnosis and when clinically indicated (associated autoimmune disease).
Screen for depression, diabetes distress, disordered eating (including insulin omission) and alcohol or drug use; offer psychological support.
Manage blood pressure, lipids and smoking actively: cardiovascular risk is increased in type 1 diabetes.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Labelling a lean young adult, or an older adult with rapid weight loss, as type 2 and starting oral agents: check antibodies.
Stopping basal insulin during illness, fasting or vomiting, precipitating DKA.
Stopping insulin during the honeymoon phase: doses fall but insulin must continue.
Using correction (sliding-scale) insulin alone without basal insulin.
Overtreating hypoglycaemia by relying on CGM readings that lag behind blood glucose.

drugs.name: Basal insulin analogue (glargine U100, degludec)
drugs.dose: About 50% of the total daily dose SC once daily (TDD typically 0.5 units/kg/day at start)
drugs.notes: Never omit on sick days. Detemir may need twice-daily dosing.

drugs.name: Rapid-acting insulin analogue (aspart, lispro, glulisine)
drugs.dose: About 50% of the total daily dose divided between meals, SC 0 to 15 minutes before eating, dosed by insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio plus correction
drugs.notes: Ultra-rapid analogues can be given at the start of the meal.

drugs.name: NPH plus regular human insulin
drugs.dose: NPH SC twice daily as basal insulin, with regular insulin SC 30 minutes before meals
drugs.notes: Lower-cost alternative when analogues are unavailable; more hypoglycaemia, especially overnight.

drugs.name: Glucose (oral)
drugs.dose: 15 g orally for glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), repeated every 15 minutes until above 70 mg/dL
drugs.notes: 5 to 15 g often suffices with AID. Follow with about 20 g carbohydrate.

drugs.name: Glucagon
drugs.dose: 1 mg IM or SC, or nasal glucagon 3 mg, for level 3 hypoglycaemia when oral intake is unsafe
drugs.notes: Prescribe to all people on insulin; train family members.
